chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from al-Halabi, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, when I completed my ritual sacrifice for the 'Umrah, I returned to my family and did not shorten (my journey).' He said, 'Upon you is a camel.'

I said, 'When I intended to take her (the camel) for the sacrifice, she had not shortened (her journey), so she refused. When I overpowered her, she bit off some of her hair with her teeth.' He said, 'May Allah have mercy on her, she was more juristic than you. Upon you is a camel, and there is nothing upon her.'

key_terms.بَدَنَةٌ: a camel (specifically a female camel used for sacrifice)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim who completes the 'Umrah sacrifice but does not shorten their journey?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the ruling for a pilgrim who performs *Tamattu'* or *Qiran* but fails to shorten their journey (by cutting hair) before the sacrifice, mandating a camel (*badanah*) as compensation. The Imam’s witty remark that the camel was 'more learned' (*afqaha*) than the pilgrim, because it avoided the slaughter by biting its own hair, highlights the distinction between the animal's exemption and the human's obligation. This incident underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that the validity of the sacrifice is not invalidated by the pilgrim's failure to perform the subsequent ritual haircut, though the penalty remains on the pilgrim.
